record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: For soft glassy materials that show non-monotonic stress relaxation after flow cessation, what minimal microscopic ingredients are required, what roles are played by colloid shape, deformability, and non-central interparticle forces, can systems denser than gels and polymer solutions such as soft repulsive glasses show the same relaxation, and can coarse-grained elastoplastic models capture the interplay of these ingredients?

evidence.quote: Yet, numerous issues remain open, including (i) the minimal microscopic ingredients needed to observe a non-monotonic relaxation, (ii) the role of the shape of the colloids, their deformability , 199 and of the nature of interparticle (non-central) forces in such an anomalous relaxation, and (iii) the possibility for systems denser than gels and polymer solutions, e.g., soft repulsive glasses, to display similar stress relaxation. The interplay of these different ingredients could be naturally investigated in coarse-grained descriptions such as elasto-plastic models.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a soft amorphous material consisting of mesoscopic constituents (e.g., colloids, droplets, or soft particles) subjected to an imposed shear deformation that is suddenly stopped (flow cessation). After cessation, the macroscopic shear stress σ(t) relaxes toward an asymptotic value. In several experimental soft systems, σ(t) is observed to be non-monotonic: it first decreases, then partially re-increases, before finally relaxing. Investigate the following questions:

(a) Determine the minimal set of microscopic ingredients (particle interactions, internal degrees of freedom, structural features) that a microscopic or particle-based model must include in order to reproduce a non-monotonic post-cessation stress relaxation σ(t).

(b) Quantify the respective roles played in this anomalous relaxation by (i) the geometric shape of the constituent particles, (ii) their deformability (e.g., soft elastic vs. rigid particles), and (iii) the presence of non-central interparticle forces (tangential, frictional, or torque-bearing contacts), and identify which of these ingredients are necessary and which are merely sufficient.

(c) Decide whether systems denser than gels and semidilute polymer solutions — in particular soft repulsive glasses above the colloidal glass transition — can exhibit the same non-monotonic stress relaxation after flow cessation, and characterize the conditions (volume fraction, interaction softness, prior shear history) under which they do or do not.

(d) Construct a coarse-grained elastoplastic model — i.e., a mesoscopic lattice or continuum description in which local elastic blocks accumulate stress, yield plastically above a local threshold, and elastically redistribute stress via an Eshelby-like propagator — that incorporates the ingredients identified in (a)–(c), and determine whether such a model can quantitatively reproduce non-monotonic post-cessation stress relaxation and capture the interplay between particle shape, deformability, and non-central forces.
artifact.status_search_result: The question concerns a set of open issues on non-monotonic stress relaxation after flow cessation in soft amorphous materials. Recent reviews and research articles on yielding and elastoplastic modeling of soft glasses (2023–2025) continue to list the microscopic origin of non-monotonic post-cessation relaxation, the roles of particle shape/deformability/non-central forces, and the extension to dense soft repulsive glasses as unresolved, with elastoplastic models so far only partially capturing such anomalous behavior. No definitive resolution was found.
